questions.q: Define scarcity in economics. How does it differ from a shortage?
questions.a: Scarcity is a permanent, universal condition where resources are insufficient to satisfy all human wants; a shortage is a temporary market imbalance where quantity demanded exceeds quantity supplied at a given price. A wrong answer (e.g., "scarcity means shortage") reveals confusion between a fundamental economic problem and a market disequilibrium — the student has not grasped that scarcity exists even in well-supplied markets.

questions.q: "Opportunity cost is the money you spend on a choice." Explain why this statement is incorrect using the concept of implicit costs.
questions.a: Opportunity cost includes both explicit (monetary) and implicit (non-monetary) costs — e.g., a student choosing college over a ₹3 lakh/year job incurs ₹3 lakh implicit cost (foregone earnings) plus tuition (explicit). A wrong answer reveals the student equates cost only with out-of-pocket expenditure, ignoring the value of the next best alternative — a critical error for PPF and comparative advantage problems.

questions.q: A factory has 100 machine-hours and 50 labour-hours daily. It produces two goods: A (requires 2 machine-hours, 1 labour-hour per unit) and B (requires 1 machine-hour, 2 labour-hours per unit). If the factory currently produces 20 units of A and 10 units of B, calculate the opportunity cost of producing 5 more units of A in terms of B forgone, assuming full resource utilisation.
questions.a: Current usage: A=20 → 40 machine-hrs, 20 labour-hrs; B=10 → 10 machine-hrs, 20 labour-hrs. Total used: 50 machine-hrs, 40 labour-hrs. Slack: 50 machine-hrs, 10 labour-hrs. To produce 5 more A: needs 10 machine-hrs, 5 labour-hrs — feasible within slack. Opportunity cost = 0 units of B (no trade-off yet). If instead at full capacity (e.g., 30A, 10B uses 70 machine, 50 labour), 5 more A needs 10 machine, 5 labour → must reduce B by 5 units (releases 5 machine, 10 labour). Opportunity cost = 5 units of B. A wrong answer (e.g., "5 units of B" without checking slack) reveals failure to verify binding constraints — a common error in linear programming and PPF questions.

questions.q: Compare how scarcity manifests for a household versus the Government of India. Use the concepts of budget constraint and fiscal deficit in your answer.
questions.a: A household faces a hard budget constraint: spending ≤ income + borrowing; choices are private (consumption vs saving). The Government faces a softer constraint: it can borrow (fiscal deficit), print money (inflation tax), or tax — but scarcity still binds because resources (labour, capital, natural) are finite. A wrong answer (e.g., "government has no scarcity because it prints money") ignores that printing money doesn't create real resources — it redistributes purchasing power, causing inflation. This confusion undermines understanding of fiscal policy limits (c12_eco_cbse_01_008, c12_eco_cbse_01_009).

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "If India discovers a massive new oil reserve, the problem of scarcity is solved." Consider both micro and macro perspectives.
questions.a: False. The discovery alleviates *one* resource constraint (energy) but scarcity persists: (a) oil is still finite and extraction has opportunity cost (land, labour, capital, environment); (b) other resources (water, skilled labour, clean air) remain scarce; (c) at macro level, new revenue creates new allocation choices (Dutch disease, inflation, inequality). A wrong answer ("yes, scarcity solved") reveals a misunderstanding that scarcity is about *all* resources relative to *all* wants, not a single commodity — and ignores dynamic wants expansion.

questions.q: Construct a real-life scenario involving a Class 12 student choosing between three activities on a Sunday: (a) studying Economics for 4 hours, (b) working a part-time tutoring job earning ₹500, (c) attending a cricket match with friends. Identify the opportunity cost of each choice and explain how the concept of "margin" applies.
questions.a: If the student chooses (a), opportunity cost = max(₹500, enjoyment of match). If (b), opportunity cost = max(grade improvement from 4 hrs study, match enjoyment). If (c), opportunity cost = max(₹500, grade improvement). At the margin, the student compares *additional* benefit of 1 more hour of study vs 1 more hour of work/leisure. A good answer explicitly ranks alternatives and recognises opportunity cost is the *next best* (not sum of all). A poor answer lists all forgone options as cost — revealing confusion between opportunity cost and total forgone alternatives.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Scarcity is the ______ economic condition where unlimited human wants exceed the limited resources available to satisfy them, forcing every economic agent (individuals, firms, government) to make choices involving trade-offs; each choice incurs an opportunity cost — the value of the next best alternative forgone.
Fill in the blank: Imagine a farmer in Punjab with 10 hectares of land, ______ groundwater, and ₹5 lakh capital deciding between wheat and rice cultivation for the rabi season.
What is Scarcity? State the definition given in this lesson.
questions.a: Scarcity is the fundamental economic condition where unlimited human wants exceed the limited resources available to satisfy them, forcing every economic agent (individuals, firms, government) to make choices involving trade-offs; each choice incurs an opportunity cost — the value of the next best alternative forgone.

questions.q: What common mix-up does this lesson flag about Scarcity?
questions.a: Students believe scarcity only applies to "poor" people or countries — "rich people don't face scarcity." In reality, even a billionaire faces scarcity of *time* (24 hours/day), *attention*, and *unique* resources (e.g., a specific vintage wine, a Nobel Prize).

questions.q: What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why scarcity is the root cause of all economic problems, distinguish between wants and needs in a resource-constrained context, and articulate how opportunity cost arises from every choice using a Production Possibility Frontier (PPF) example with numerical data.
